extraction.name: MMMU: A Massive Multi-discipline Multimodal Understanding and Reasoning Benchmark for Expert AGI
extraction.description: MMMU is a benchmark designed to evaluate multimodal models on massive multi-discipline tasks demanding college-level subject knowledge and deliberate reasoning. It includes 11.5K meticulously collected multimodal questions from college exams, quizzes, and textbooks, covering six core disciplines: Art & Design, Business, Science, Health & Medicine, Humanities & Social Science, and Tech & Engineering. These questions span 30 subjects and 183 subfields, comprising 30 highly heterogeneous image types, such as charts, diagrams, maps, tables, music sheets, and chemical structures.

extraction.rai:dataCollection: The benchmark collection took three stages. First, common university majors were reviewed to decide which subjects to include, selecting 30 subjects from six disciplines based on the principle that visual inputs should be commonly adopted. Second, over 50 university students (including co-authors) specializing in these majors were recruited as annotators to collect multimodal questions from major textbooks and online resources, creating new questions based on their expertise where necessary. Annotators were instructed to adhere to copyright and license regulations and to select questions without immediately available answers to avoid data contamination. This process resulted in a diverse collection of 13K questions.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Manual Human Curator, Document analysis, Web Scraping
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Multimodal questions collected from college exams, quizzes, textbooks, free online resources, and lecture materials across 30 subjects and 6 disciplines.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Questions were categorized into four difficulty levels: very easy, easy, medium, and hard. Approximately 10% of the problems, classified as very easy and not aligning with the design criteria, were excluded from the benchmark.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Two steps of data cleaning were performed. First, lexical overlap and source URL similarity were employed to identify potential duplicate problems, which were then reviewed by authors to eliminate duplications. Second, problems were distributed among co-authors for format and typo checking, ensuring adherence to a standardized format. Finally, problems were categorized by difficulty and approximately 10% classified as very easy were excluded.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Over 50 university students specializing in the relevant majors were recruited as annotators. They collected multimodal questions from major textbooks and online resources, and created new questions based on their expertise where necessary. Annotators were instructed to adhere to copyright and licensing regulations, avoid data from sites prohibiting copy and redistribution, and select questions without immediately available answers. All questions must contain one or more images, be written in English, meet college-level difficulty, and not be ambiguous. Annotations included fields for question type, question text, answer options (for multiple-choice), correct answer, image types, question difficulty, and explanation (if available). A secondary review team vetted annotations for quality and guideline adherence, and regular audits of random samples were conducted.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: A user-friendly web interface for data annotation and verification was developed by Tianyu Zheng.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Ambiguities or unclear data instances were flagged for detailed review and collaboratively examined in team meetings to establish a standardized approach. A secondary review team rigorously vetted annotations for quality and guideline adherence. Regular audits of random samples from the dataset were conducted to ensure sustained quality and consistency.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Over 50 university students (including co-authors) from various disciplines and subjects, specializing in the relevant majors. 3 student experts per subject were involved in human expert evaluation (90 college senior students total for the validation set).
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The dataset has a live-updating leaderboard available at https://mmmu-benchmark.github.io/#leaderboard. The dataset has gone through multiple versions (V1 released Nov. 27, 2023; V2 Dec. 18, 2023; V3 Dec. 21, 2023; V4 June 13, 2024) with updates including new model results, bug fixes, and corrections.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: MMMU is designed to monitor progress towards Expert AGI, defined as AI systems reaching at least the 90th percentile of skilled adults in a broad range of tasks. The benchmark is intended to stimulate the community to build next-generation multimodal foundation models. The authors caution that achieving Expert AGI could lead to significant risks of job displacement and economic disruption, and that it is of both intellectual and societal importance to closely monitor progress towards Expert AGI.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The manual curation process may carry biases. GPT-4V error analysis revealed that the model often exhibits a bias towards text, prioritizing textual information over visual inputs. The benchmark's focus on college-level subjects might not be sufficient for testing Expert AGI. Open-source models demonstrate relatively strong performance in categories like Photos and Paintings, which are more frequently seen during training, but perform poorly on less common image categories.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: MMMU is not a sufficient test for Expert AGI, as there lacks a direct mapping between performance on MMMU and '90th percentile of skilled adults,' nor are college exams the only tasks an AGI shall tackle. The focus on college-level subjects might not be sufficient for testing Expert AGI. The manual curation process may carry biases. Some subjects like law and linguistics were excluded because it was difficult to find enough relevant multimodal problems.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is designed for evaluating (testing) multimodal foundation models on expert-level multimodal understanding and reasoning tasks. It includes a few-shot development set (5 questions per subject), a validation set (~900 questions) useful for hyperparameter selection, and a test set (10,500 questions). It can be used to measure three essential skills in LMMs: perception, knowledge, and reasoning. The benchmark is intended to monitor progress towards Expert AGI and stimulate development of next-generation multimodal foundation models.
